en: The Scripture on the Dispelling of Sorrow Spoken by the Buddha,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Proclaimed Great Officer, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial,
and Grand Master for the Propagation of the Teaching, the Subject Fata, by Imperial Decree.
I bow my head in refuge to the Perfectly Awakened One, Who can ferry beings across the boundless great ocean of suffering.
Constantly moistening all living beings with the nectar of immortality, And enabling them to attain nirvana—to you I prostrate.
I prostrate and take refuge in the Treasury of the True Dharma, Which can cease the causes of boundless suffering and affliction;
Revealing the transcendence of gain and loss for the benefit of sentient beings, I pay homage to that which brings about the attainment of tranquility.
I bow my head in refuge to the Great Bhikṣu, Who is able to provide for the world a mass of merit;
To him who initiates practice and diligently cultivates the causes of peace and happiness, And who skillfully severs the cycle of saṃsāra, I prostrate.
Separation from those one loves is the greatest suffering; The fire of grief constantly burns.
If you wish to find peace of mind, Sit upright and practice contemplation.
Just as flocks of birds and herds of beasts Gather for a moment and then fly apart, each in its own direction.
It is the same for those who pass through birth and death; why then harbor grief and suffering?
Only the individual dies, while the multitude continue to live;
the pain of parting is unbearable, and kinsmen must weep.
In the great saṃsāra of the three realms, there is none who can escape this;
all equally undergo impermanence—why then harbor grief and suffering?
If a person gives rise to craving and attachment, who would realize they are being burned by the fire of greed?
Just as that yak, out of love for its tail, meets its death at the hands of man;
so too do many people in the world remain mired in delusion and intoxication.
Though they devise every possible expedient to escape the perilous and evil path, they are unable to free themselves from suffering.
Like those wild deer in the wilderness, constantly pursued by lions, who ultimately cannot escape— why harbor such sorrow and suffering?
Whether upon the great earth or in the heavens, within the three realms and the four modes of birth, [all are subject to this].
Never before have I seen or heard of one who does not undergo impermanence.
It is like a wildfire in the mountains and fields; when it burns away the grasses and trees, it makes no distinction between flowers, fruits, or forests, reducing them all simultaneously to ashes.
Foolish sentient beings, through their perversions, give rise to delusive thoughts;
bound by the rope of impermanence, no one can untie them.
Within the Brahma worlds of the realm of form, they take the flavor of dhyāna to be true peace and bliss.
Just as a tree standing by a river will soon be destroyed by wind and water,
so too are the billions of universal wheel-turning kings and the millions of Śakras, lords of the gods;
in every thought-moment they are impermanent, like the flickering flame of a lamp blown by the wind.
The great seers of the past, Whose minds were sovereign and possessed the five supernormal powers,
Who traveled back and forth soaring through the air, Were nonetheless seized by impermanence.
Even those with bodies as firm as adamant Still manifested their entry into parinirvāṇa.
All consciousness is like a plantain tree; how could it be expected to endure long?
The great earth, Mount Sumeru, and the four great oceans—even these will return to emptiness when the kalpa is destroyed— how much more so the realms of sentient beings!
A dragon dwelling in the deep ocean is constantly surrounded by its kin;
yet when the golden-winged bird can devour it, the suffering of separation is likewise the same.
Or when a person goes to another realm, desiring to avoid impermanence—
Like entering the mouth of a makara fish seeking safety,
so it is within the realm of desire and the realm of form, as well as that of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
there is not a single thing that is not swallowed by impermanence.
Only the Perfectly Awakened One is the true place of reliance;
believe this and listen attentively, for it can resolve all sorrows and afflictions.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Sentient beings are innumerable and their saṃsāra is boundless; they revolve like ants in a circle, without end."
Sentient beings, gripped by craving and obstructed by ignorance, are like those mired in mud, unable to emerge.
The number of times sentient beings have transmigrated and returned through the cycle of rebirth in the past cannot be known.
"O Bhikṣus!

Suppose all the soil of the great earth were gathered together and kneaded into a single lump of clay, the size of a pea. If one were to place a single lump of clay for every parent, child, or grandchild of those sentient beings born throughout beginningless kalpas, even when all such lumps of clay had been exhausted, the number of parents, children, and grandchildren would still not have reached its end."
"O Bhikṣus!

Thus, these infinite sentient beings in saṃsāra, through craving and ignorance, fall into the mire of inverted desires and revolve in birth and death, their number unknown. For this reason, I cause you to train in severing saṃsāra."
The Buddha said, "Bhikṣus!
If the bones of such individuals who have transmigrated through saṃsāra were gathered into a heap, it would be like Mount Sumeru, neither decaying nor rotting."

In this way, the śrāvaka who is beyond training realizes the Four Noble Truths; he understands that this suffering is truly suffering, and having realized the cessation of suffering, he realizes the Noble Truth of Suffering.
That person, seeing these skeletal remains, does not recognize them as suffering, nor can they extinguish the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms.
If one were to extinguish the afflictions of the three realms and realize the non-empty Dharma of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), one would certainly attain enlightenment (*bodhi*).
Because they sever the cycle of rebirth and eliminate the afflictions (*kleśa*) among seven births as gods or humans, once these seven births are completed, the Noble Truths manifest before them;
through the wisdom of right view, they extinguish all remaining delusions and reach the tranquility of *nirvāṇa*. Only then does that *pudgala* attain liberation from the suffering of saṃsāra!
The Buddha said,
“Bhikṣus! It is like a family of relatives who love and delight in one another.”
Due to craving and attachment, they extensively create various karmas and undergo the cycle of birth and death.
It is like a wild elephant fallen into a pit of mud, with no time of emergence in sight.
Furthermore, their retinues are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; their parents raise and nurture them all as if they were their own children.

In future lives, according to their respective retributions, they will each experience different conditions—some becoming servants, others becoming enemies, harboring mutual resentment, and subjecting one another to humiliation, beating, and abuse;

or becoming animals of various kinds, preying upon one another, or being slaughtered. Such are the various cycles of rebirth in the realms of existence, like the seven celestial seers who gather and disperse, or like rain from the heavens that produces bubbles of water, which arise and perish.
Such sentient beings possess the great power of ignorance; deluded and inverted, they do not understand saṃsāra.
Regarding their own kin, they falsely conceive the notion of happiness, creating various kinds of karma, without ever for a single moment attaining a state of pure abiding.
"Furthermore, those sentient beings, wandering in saṃsāra from beginningless time, have drunk more molten copper while inside the hells than there is water in the great oceans;
they have consumed impure things like swine and dogs, as much as Mount Sumeru."
Furthermore, the tears shed by those sentient beings when separated from one another through birth and death, out of love and longing, are equal to the waters of the great ocean.

Moreover, the heads of those sentient beings who have killed and harmed one another, piled up until they exceed the realm of Brahmā and are devoured by worms amidst pus and blood, are also equal to the waters of the great ocean.

Furthermore, in the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), due to past stinginess and greed, they undergo the sufferings of hunger and thirst; should they encounter food or drink, it immediately turns into smoke and flames.

Once their karmic retribution as a ghost is exhausted, even if they are born among humans, they will experience poverty, hunger, exhaustion, and various other afflictions that cannot be fully described.
Furthermore, those sentient beings, having cultivated meritorious virtues, are born in superior realms such as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where they constantly experience happiness;
yet their craving blazes intensely like fire consuming dry grass, and when their karmic lifespan is exhausted, they immediately fall into the evil destinies.
For example, just as a bird whose two wings are broken falls to the ground in an instant and undergoes manifold sufferings,
so too should you all train to sever saṃsāra and swiftly seek liberation.
The Buddha said, “Bhikṣus! It is as if the rivers,
the great earth, the sun and moon, the stars and constellations, Mount Sumeru, and all the villages and worlds were not to perish, but would endure for a long time, remaining forever in the world.”
This present sutra is likewise so: as long as the world has not yet been destroyed, the Dharma shall also abide for a long time.
What do you think?
It is for the sake of bringing rest to all sentient beings from saṃsāra.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly. Thus spoke the Buddha in the *Sāntarakṣa-sūtra* (The Discourse on the Dispelling of Sorrow).
